terms.comment: Fussiness itself is fastīdium, and to turn up one’s nose at a thing, fastīdīre: quod fastīdit quisque, what each one won’t eat (Phaedr. 3.7.23).

evidence: Suet. Jul. 45: circā corporis cūram mōrōsior (Lewis & Short: “particular, fastidious”)
terms.comment: Often “grumpy” as well (see “difficult”, of a person).

phrases.latin: Antōnius, quī maximē expetēbātur, facilis in causīs recipiendīs erat; fastīdiōsior Crassus, sed tamen recipiēbat.
phrases.english: Antonius, who was most in demand, was easy-going about taking on cases; Crassus was more particular, but took them all the same.

phrases.latin: usque eō difficilēs ac mōrōsī sumus, ut nōbīs nōn satis faciat ipse Dēmosthenēs
phrases.english: we are so particular and hard to please that not even Demosthenes satisfies us
tasting a little of everything is the mark of a fussy stomach

sources: Lewis & Short: fastidiosus · Lewis & Short: morosus · Lewis & Short: delicatus · Lewis & Short: fastidio
